title: More Japanese Teens Getting Cosmetic Surgery
paragraphs: A growing number of young people in Japan, including those under the age of 20, are having cosmetic surgery, according to a recent report by Jiji Press.

At 17 clinics run by Kyoritsu Cosmetic Surgery, a major cosmetic surgery group, the share of patients aged 19 or younger has risen sharply. In 2017, they made up 7.2% of all patients, but by 2025, this figure had climbed to 18.8%.

One of the most popular procedures among young people is double eyelid surgery, which creates a fold in the upper eyelid. Among patients under 20 at the Kyoritsu clinics, the share having this surgery rose from 18.8% in 2018 to 27.2% in 2025.

There are two main ways of carrying out the surgery. In the most common method, the doctor passes a thread through the eyelid to create a fold, without cutting the skin. This method causes little swelling, and the thread can be removed later. In the other method, the doctor uses a scalpel to cut along the line where the fold will be. The operation takes about 30 minutes, and it takes about a month for the eyelid to look natural.

According to Kim Ahmi, a doctor at Shonan Beauty Clinic in Tokyo's Shinjuku district, young people's consultations are concentrated during the summer vacation and before they enter high school. The clinic has even treated children who had just graduated from elementary school. Kim said that there are no particular physical risks for minors.

In Japan, patients under 18 must be accompanied by a parent or guardian, whose permission is required. In some cases, minors have surgery because their parents want them to. For example, manga artist Gura Hamuco had her first eyelid surgery during junior high school after her mother suggested it. She said there is certainly hidden pressure from society that people should be beautiful.

Akihito Kujime of the Japan Association of Aesthetic Medicine said that while it is important to respect young patients' wishes, doctors and parents should listen carefully to them before surgery. Kujime also said doctors should avoid procedures that cannot be reversed, such as shaving bones.
